title: Reading Python error messages
prompt: Read a traceback from the bottom up, and recognise the handful of errors you'll actually hit.

thumbnail.question:

this red text?

segments.text: Welcome back to Basic Python, episode ten. This is a short one, but it might genuinely be the most useful six minutes in the whole course. Because here is the truth about programming. Your code will break. Constantly. Every single day that you do this, for the rest of your life. The difference between a frustrating wasted hour, and a two minute fix, is almost entirely whether you can read the error message that Python gives you. Beginners tend to do one of two things when they see a wall of red text. They panic and start randomly changing lines, or they scroll past it and ignore it. But that red text is not noise. It is Python telling you, very precisely, what went wrong, and where. So let's learn to actually read it.

segments.cardSubtitle: what all that red text means

segments.text: When Python hits an error it cannot deal with, it prints something called a traceback, and then it stops. Let's look at a real one. This little program tries to print a variable called nam, but we actually named it name, up on the first line. A typo. The very first line of the traceback just says, Traceback, most recent call last. That is a fixed header, the same every time, ignore it. Then a block showing a file name, a line number, and the actual line of code from your file, here line two, print of nam. That block is Python pointing at exactly where it was standing when everything went wrong. And then the final line, the one you should read first. NameError, colon, name nam is not defined. That last line is the diagnosis, and it has two parts. The error type, NameError, which is a category. And a plain English explanation, nam is not defined, the specifics. Read as a sentence, it says, on line two you used something called nam, and there is no such thing anywhere. Which is exactly right. The fix is obvious once you have actually read the message.

segments.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "solution.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(nam)
NameError: name 'nam' is not defined. Did you mean: 'name'?

segments.text: Notice Python even took a guess at the end. Did you mean, name. Recent versions of Python are genuinely helpful like this, offering the likely fix for common typos, so always read the whole message, right to the end. And here is the one rule for reading any traceback, no matter how long. Start at the bottom. The last line is the what. The block just above it is the where. If the traceback is really long, with many file blocks stacked up, that is the whole chain of function calls that led to the crash, and the one you usually care about is the lowest block that is still in a file you wrote, not one buried deep inside some library.

segments.cardSubtitle: you'll meet these again and again

segments.text: The good news is you have already met most of the errors you are going to hit, scattered across the last few episodes. Let's name them, all in one place. A NameError means you used a variable or function name that does not exist. Almost always a typo, or using something before the line that defines it. A TypeError means you did an operation on the wrong type of thing, like adding a string to a number. A ValueError means the type was right but the value was not acceptable. The classic is int of the word hello, a string was fine, but that particular string is not a number.

Continuing the list. An IndexError means you asked a list or a string for a position that is out of range, like index ten in a six item list. A KeyError means you asked a dictionary for a key it does not contain. And an AttributeError means you used a dot, a method or an attribute, on something that does not have it, like calling dot append on a string. That is basically the entire cast of characters you will deal with for a long time. Here is a TypeError to practise on. Read it from the bottom. The last line says you can only join a string to a string, not an integer. The line above says line two. So, on line two, you tried to add a number to a string with a plus.

segments.error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "solution.py", line 2, in <module>
    print("age: " + age)
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

segments.text: One error type stands apart. The SyntaxError. Every other error happens while your program runs. A SyntaxError happens before it runs at all, not a single line executes, because Python could not make sense of your code as valid Python in the first place. A missing colon after an if or a for. An unclosed bracket or quote. Because nothing ran, it has no chain of function calls, just a file, a line number, and a little caret pointing at roughly where Python gave up. And here is the catch that wastes people's time. The line it reports is where Python noticed the problem, which is very often the line after the real mistake. Forget a closing bracket at the end of line one, and Python keeps reading onto line two still looking for it, then blames line two. So with any SyntaxError, always check the line above the one it points at, and count your brackets and quotes.

segments.error:
File "solution.py", line 2
    print(total)
    ^^^^^
SyntaxError: '(' was never closed

the real problem is the missing ) on line 1.

segments.question: You get a traceback. Which line tells you WHAT went wrong?
segments.answer: The last line — the error type and its plain-English message. Always read bottom-up.

segments.text: Do not be afraid of the red text. It is the most honest, most useful feedback you will ever get as a programmer. Read it from the bottom up. The last line is the diagnosis, the type and the explanation. The lines above it are the location. Learn the six or so common error types and what each one means. And with a SyntaxError, remember to look one line up from where it points. Next episode, instead of just reading errors after they happen, we learn to catch them and handle them gracefully, with try and except.

points: read a traceback from the BOTTOM: last line = what went wrong, lines above = where
NameError = typo / undefined; TypeError = wrong type; ValueError = right type, bad value
IndexError = position out of range; KeyError = missing dict key; AttributeError = no such method
SyntaxError happens before anything runs, and often points one line too late — check the line above
recent Python often suggests the fix ('Did you mean...') — read the whole message
